newsitem.title: USA: Glickman urges House to leave sugar, peanuts alone.
newsitem.headline: Glickman urges House to leave sugar, peanuts alone.

text.p: U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman urged House lawmakers not to alter the sugar and peanut programs during their work Thursday on the fiscal 1998 agriculture department spending bill.
"I do not believe we want to change a farm program in an appropriations bill," Glickman told reporters after a speech Thursday to USDA overseas staff here for an annual conference.

But the House should restore funding for the salaries of two USDA officials who have been caught in a controversy over the recent Conservation Reserve Program enrollment results in Washington state, he said.
Glickman said he opposes an amendment that would eliminate federal crop insurance for tobacco growers.
Of all the anti-farm program amendments, the one eliminating federal crop insurance for tobacco growers might have the best chance of success, a House Republican aide said.
"There's some feeling some members want to put a marker down on tobacco," the aide said.

Last month, a group of state attorney generals reached a $368.5 billion settlement with tobacco companies. With that pact now facing an uncertain fate in Congress, many members want to demonstrate a tough stance on tobacco, the aide said.

A sugar amendment to be offered by Rep. Dan Miller, a Florida Republican, and others would eliminate USDA's authority to offer non-recourse loans to sugar processors. Those loans allow processors to forfeit sugar stocks to the government in lieu of repayment.

Sugar growers contend that eliminating non-recourse loan would impair the price support function of the sugar loan program and are cautiously optimistic they have rallied enough support in the House to defeat the measure.
The peanut amendment would effectively cap domestic peanut prices at $550 per short ton, well below the minimum price support level of $610 approved in the 1996 farm bill.
Peanut program critics contend that the reforms made last year haven't reduced domestic prices as much as expected.
Currently, the spending bill contains a provision that would eliminate funding for the salaries of the deputy administrator and the assistant deputy administrator of the Farm Service Agency.

The House Appropriations Committee included that language at the request of Rep. George Nethercutt, a Washington Republican, who is upset about the low amount of acres enrolled in the CRP in his state this past spring compared with surrounding states.

Under the CRP, farmers receive an annual payment to keep land out of production to acheive certain environmental objectives like providing wildlife habitat, reducing soil erosion and enhancing air and water quality.

Only about 20 percent of the land offered by farmers in Washington was enrolled, compared to about 80 percent in surrounding states. Nethercutt blames the two individuals in question for rejecting a plan to boost Washington's enrollment.
In a letter to members of Congress, Glickman said he "strongly supported" an amendment to restore funding for the two positions.

"While I recognize there are legitimate policy differences regarding the acreage that was accepted during the recent CRP signup, I'm disappointed that this issue has been personalized through the singling out of two Department employees," he said.
